editorial.headline: Fitness Clubs: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers professional, semi-professional and amateur fitness and bodybuilding clubs—but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium changes the practical answer for foreign investors.
editorial.body:
A fitness club under this activity is not simply a room of equipment or a branded exercise concept. It is an organisation or club—professional, semi-professional or amateur—that gives its members the opportunity to take part in sport. That opportunity may be supported by a dedicated venue and sporting facilities, or it may be organised without either. The defining feature is the club’s role in enabling member participation in fitness, exercise and bodybuilding activity.

The activity is open to small, medium and large business scales. Nationally, it is classified as open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. For an investor assessing the Indonesian position in isolation, that is a clear result: the activity is available for PMA registration at every listed scale, with no national foreign-equity cap below full ownership stated in the record.

Bali requires a more exact reading. A foreign investor cannot register this activity at a Bali address today. The record marks it closed under Bali’s PMA moratorium because the large scale is treated as medium-low risk. The provincial rule blocks all low- and medium-low-risk activities from PMA registration across the island, permanently. This is not a marginal procedural qualification to an otherwise open national classification; it determines whether the foreign-owned structure can be registered in Bali.

That distinction is the central planning fact. The national framework says the activity is open and permits up to 100% foreign ownership. Bali’s provincial position nonetheless closes PMA registration for this activity at a Bali address under the moratorium. A club operator can therefore understand the activity’s commercial scope and its national investment openness without confusing either with a current route to foreign-owned registration in Bali. The two positions must be read together: national openness describes the ceiling; the Bali moratorium decides the local outcome.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness permits up to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s moratorium closes PMA registration for this activity at a Bali address.
